title: Every Word at Once: How Attention Replaced Reading in Order
audience: A curious adult with no background in this field

source.title: Attention Is All You Need
source.authors: Ashish Vaswani, Noam Shazeer, Niki Parmar, Jakob Uszkoreit, Llion Jones, Aidan N. Gomez, Łukasz Kaiser, Illia Polosukhin
source.venue: 31st Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NIPS 2017)

intro.summary: In 2017 the best machine translation systems read a sentence one word at a time, passing a running summary from each word to the next. This paper asks whether that step-by-step reading is needed at all. The authors built the Transformer, a network in which every word looks directly at every other word in a single step, using a mechanism called attention. On two standard English-to-German and English-to-French translation tests it scored better than earlier systems while training in a fraction of the time. The tests cover translation and one grammar-parsing task, scored mostly by an automatic metric called BLEU. The method's cost also grows with the square of sentence length, so very long inputs remain expensive.
background: Neural networks are programs that learn their behaviour by adjusting millions of numbers until their outputs match many training examples.
Before a network can work with words, each word is turned into a list of numbers called a vector, so that similar words get similar lists.
Translation quality is often scored with BLEU, which measures how much a machine translation overlaps with human translations; higher is better.
Graphics chips (GPUs) are fast because they do thousands of calculations at the same time, but only when those calculations don't have to wait for one another.
intro.aha: A translator that never reads a sentence in order, letting every word look straight at every other word in one step, beat the best step-by-step systems while training in a fraction of the time.

primer.heading: The question
primer.body: Translation systems in 2017 mostly used recurrent networks. A recurrent network reads a sentence like a person reading aloud: word one, then word two, carrying a memory forward each time. Each step must wait for the step before it, so this kind of reading can't be spread across a GPU's many parallel workers, and long sentences are slow to train on. The authors asked whether a network could skip the word-by-word reading entirely.
primer.quote: This inherently sequential nature precludes parallelization within training examples, which becomes critical at longer sequence lengths, as memory constraints limit batching across examples.

primer.heading: What they did
primer.body: They built a network called the Transformer around a single mechanism, attention. Each word asks a question, compares it with a label on every other word, and gathers information mostly from the words that match best. This happens for all words at the same moment. The network runs several of these attention 'heads' side by side and adds a wave-based position signal so it still knows word order. They trained it on millions of sentence pairs and compared it with the best existing systems.
primer.quote: We propose a new simple network architecture, the Transformer, based solely on attention mechanisms, dispensing with recurrence and convolutions entirely.

primer.heading: What they found
primer.body: With no step-by-step reading at all, the Transformer translated better than every earlier system on the English-to-German test, including combinations of several models. It also needed far less computing to train: the smaller version trained in about 12 hours on eight GPUs. The same design also did well on a different task, parsing the grammar of English sentences.
primer.quote: Our model achieves 28.4 BLEU on the WMT 2014 English-to-German translation task, improving over the existing best results, including ensembles, by over 2 BLEU.

primer.heading: Why it matters, and its limits
primer.body: Removing the word-by-word bottleneck made the network far easier to run in parallel, which made much larger training runs practical. That design choice is a big reason later language systems became possible. The evidence here has limits, though. It comes from two translation benchmarks and one parsing task, scored mainly by BLEU. Attention compares every word with every other word, so its cost grows quickly with input length, and the authors left very long inputs to future work.

concepts.title: Reading one word at a time
concepts.idea: A recurrent network must pass information along a chain, so linking two words takes as many waiting steps as there are words between them, and longer sentences mean more steps that cannot run in parallel.

predict.question: A chain reader like the one you just played with reads a 600-word document. You give it 100 times more workers than before. Roughly how many steps must still happen one after another?
options: About 6
About 60
About 600
Just 1, because every word can be read at the same moment
why: Dividing 600 by 100 workers gives 6. That is right for work with no chain, like the dashed line. The chain reader cannot split its work, because each step waits for the one before it.
This guesses that extra workers help a little but not fully. In the chain, workers do not help at all within one document, because each word's step needs the previous step's result.
Correct. One step per word, strictly in order, so about 600 steps in a row. Extra workers could handle other documents at the same time, but they cannot shorten this one's chain.
Reading every word at once would need a design with no chain. The chain reader's whole point is that word 2 waits for word 1, so it can never collapse to a single step.

terms.means: The running summary a chain reader carries forward, updated once per word
A network that reads a sequence one item at a time, feeding each new hidden state from the previous one
Steps that must happen one after another because each needs the result of the last
Splitting work so many workers or processors can do parts of it at the same moment

model.title: Steps that must wait in line as a sentence grows
model.note: Teaching model: it counts only the steps that must happen in order, one per word, as in the paper's Table 1 (O(n) steps for a sentence of n words). It ignores how long each step takes and constant factors. The 'workers' and the dashed no-chain line are an illustrative contrast, not something the paper measures. Numbers are illustrative, not the paper's data.

controls.label: Distance between two words to link

outputs.label: Steps in a row to read the sentence
Steps to carry information between the two words
Steps if the work had no chain

y.label: Steps that must happen one after another

series.label: Chain reader: one word after another
Same amount of work with no chain, split among workers

hlines.label: Steps to link the two words

steps.say: This picture counts the steps that must happen one after another as a sentence gets longer.
The solid line is a reader that takes words strictly in turn. The dot marks the sentence you are looking at.
This slider sets how many words the sentence has. Watch the dot climb the line.
This one picks two words some distance apart that the reader must connect. The flat line shows how many steps that takes.
This one adds workers who can run at the same time. The dashed line shows the same amount of work if it had no chain.

explore.prompt: Play with the chain reader. First make it link two words that are really far apart. Then see how much workers can and cannot help.

goals.text: Make linking the two words take 30 or more steps in a row
hints: Information has to travel through every word between the two linked words.
Raise the distance slider and watch the link box. Does it stop growing at some point? Why?
Two words can't be further apart than the sentence allows, so the sentence must be longer than the distance you want.

goals.text: Open a gap of more than 40 steps between the chain reader and the same work split among workers
hints: Workers only help work that has no chain.
Add workers and watch the dashed line drop while the solid line stays put. Then think about what makes the solid line tall.
You need a sentence near the top of the length range and more than a couple of workers.

feedback.correct: Right. In a chain, each word's step needs the result of the step before it. So a 600-word document means about 600 steps in a row, however many workers you add.
feedback.incorrect: It's natural to expect more workers to finish sooner. That holds for work that can be split, like the dashed line. The chain reader's steps each wait for the previous one, so within one document the count stays at one step per word.

steps.say: Start small: a five-word sentence. The reader takes word 1 and updates a running summary, then word 2, and so on. Five words, five steps in a row.
That running summary is called the hidden state. Each new hidden state is built from the previous one plus the next word. A network that works this way is a recurrent network.
Now connect word 1 to word 5. Word 1's information has to ride along the chain, handed from state to state: 4 steps.
Stretch the sentence to 30 words and link two words 25 apart. That is 25 handoffs in a row, and the information has to survive every one.
Add workers. If the work had no chain, they could share it and the dashed line falls. The solid line does not move, because each step still waits for the last.
Steps that must wait like this are called sequential operations. Their number grows with sentence length. They block parallelization, which means splitting the work across workers.
At 60 words the chain needs 60 steps in a row. The same work split among 8 workers would need about 8. That widening gap is the bottleneck.

understand.explanation: Before this paper, the leading translation systems were recurrent networks. They read a sentence one word at a time, and each new hidden state is computed from the previous one. So the number of steps that must happen in order grows with sentence length. Information from an early word must pass through every step in between to reach a later word. Extra hardware cannot shorten that chain inside one sentence: it can only run several sentences side by side, and the paper notes that memory limits how many fit when sentences are long. The paper does not test this with a new experiment. It states it as the problem that motivates its design and sums it up in Table 1 (a recurrent layer needs O(n) sequential steps and an O(n) path between distant words), citing earlier work that long paths make distant links harder to learn.
understand.quote: Aligning the positions to steps in computation time, they generate a sequence of hidden states ht, as a function of the previous hidden state ht−1 and the input for position t. This inherently sequential nature precludes parallelization within training examples, which becomes critical at longer sequence lengths, as memory constraints limit batching across examples.

connect.caption: The paper describes each hidden state h_{t} as a function of the previous state h_{t−1} and the word x_{t} at position t (Section 1). Because each h_{t} needs h_{t−1} first, a sentence of n words (the length slider) takes n steps in a row (the matching output). Table 1 records this as O(n) sequential operations for recurrent layers. The function f stands for whatever the network computes at each step; the model only counts the steps.

concepts.recap: A chain reader needs one step per word, in order, so longer sentences mean longer waits that extra hardware cannot shorten.

concepts.title: Attention: ask, match, blend
concepts.idea: Attention scores how well one word's query matches each other word's key, turns those scores into weights that sum to one (softmax), and outputs a weighted blend of the words' values.

predict.question: New case: the sentence stays the same, but every one of the four match scores goes up by exactly 2 at once. What happens to the bars?
options: Every bar grows, because every match got better
The bars stay exactly the same
The tallest bar grows and the others shrink
The bars now add up to more than 100%
why: It feels natural that better matches mean more weight. But weights are shares of one total, so all four cannot grow together.
Correct. Softmax divides each exp(score) by their sum. Adding 2 to every score multiplies every term by the same factor, and that factor cancels. Only the gaps between scores matter.
That happens when one score rises past the others. Here every gap between scores stays the same, so no word gains on any other.
Softmax always divides by the total, so the weights add to one whatever the scores are.

terms.means: The list of numbers a word uses to ask 'what am I looking for?'
The list of numbers each word offers so queries can be matched against it
The content a word hands over once it has been picked to be blended in
The rule that turns any set of scores into positive weights that add up to one: exp(score) divided by the sum of all the exp(score)s

model.title: Where does 'its' look? Match scores become shares of 100%
model.note: Teaching model: we keep four words of the paper's Figure 4 sentence ('The Law will never be perfect, but its application should be just') and show only the word 'its' looking at them, itself included. In the real Transformer each match score is computed from learned lists of 64 numbers and then divided by √64. Each word's content is also a list of 64 numbers. Here you set the scores by hand, and each word's content is one made-up number (Law 10, perfect 40, its 60, application 90). Numbers are illustrative, not the paper's data.

outputs.label: Blended content for 'its'
outputs.expr: (10 * exp(s_law) + 40 * exp(s_perfect) + 60 * exp(s_its) + 90 * exp(s_app)) / (exp(s_law) + exp(s_perfect) + exp(s_its) + exp(s_app))

steps.say: A sentence from the paper: 'The Law will never be perfect, but its application should be just.' We follow one word: 'its'.
Each bar is how much 'its' looks at that word. The four bars always share 100% between them.
Each slider says how well 'its' matches one word. Watch the 'Law' slider go up...
...the Law bar jumps, and every other bar shrinks to make room.
This number mixes the four words' content in the bar proportions. It is what 'its' carries forward.

explore.prompt: Now steer the word 'its' yourself. Shares are slices of one pie, so think about what each slider does to everyone else's slice.

goals.text: Get more than 60% of the share onto 'Law' without touching the 'Law' slider
hints: Shares are relative. If Law's own match can't rise, what else would make Law's slice bigger?
Lower the matches of the other words. Lowering 'application' alone is not enough, so check what 'perfect' and 'its' are still taking.
All three other scores need to sit somewhat below zero. Just under zero is not quite enough.

goals.text: Make 'its' split its look evenly between 'Law' and 'application', with each getting more than 40%
hints: What must be true of two scores for their bars to be the same height?
Give 'Law' and 'application' equal matches, then ask how far above 'perfect' and 'its' they must be for each to pass 40%.
Equal and only a little above the others is not enough. Push the two equal matches toward the top of their range.

feedback.correct: Right. Softmax only cares about the gaps between scores. Shift every score by the same amount and each exp(score) is multiplied by the same factor, which cancels when you divide by the total. The bars do not move.
feedback.incorrect: You probably read a higher score as more weight on its own. Weights are shares: each word's exp(score) divided by the sum over all words. If every score rises by the same amount, every term grows by the same factor, the factor cancels, and the shares stay put. Only differences between scores matter.

steps.say: Start with every match equal. Each word gets exactly 25%: 'its' spreads its look evenly, itself included.

Where do scores come from? 'its' holds a question, a list of numbers called its query. Each word holds a label, a list called its key. Multiply them entry by entry and add up: that is the match score.
Raise the Law match. A score is not a share yet. Softmax turns each score into exp(score) and divides by the total. Now Law takes about 71% and the rest share what is left.
Give 'application' the same score. Now they split, about 44% each. A strong match only wins if it beats the other matches. Being high on its own is not enough.
Drop 'application' below zero. Its share shrinks toward zero but never turns negative. Softmax keeps every share positive, and the total stays 100%.

Now the output. Each word also hands over content, called its value. Here each value is one made-up number: Law 10, perfect 40, its 60, application 90. 'its' gets the values mixed in its bar proportions.
Push 'perfect' and 'its' down too. Law takes about 87%, and the blend lands near Law's 10. The new 'its' now mostly carries the content of 'Law', the word it refers to.

understand.explanation: Attention lets one word gather information from every other word in a single step, with no chain to wait through. The word asks with its query, and each word answers with its key. Their match gives a score, and softmax turns the scores into positive shares that add to one. The word's new version is a blend of all the words' values, mixed in those shares, so it mostly takes on the content of its best match. The paper builds the whole Transformer from this operation. In its Figure 4, attention from 'its' is very sharp, in heads the authors say are 'apparently' involved in working out what a word refers to. That is their reading of a picture, not a measured test.
understand.quote: We compute the dot products of the query with all keys, divide each by √dk, and apply a softmax function to obtain the weights on the values.

connect.caption: This is the paper's Equation 1. QK^{T} holds the match scores: every query multiplied against every key, which is what your sliders stand in for. Softmax turns each row of scores into shares that add to one, like the bars and 'Share on Law'. Multiplying by V blends the values in those shares, like 'Blended content for its'. Q, K and V stack the queries, keys and values of all words, so every word does this at once. The division by √d_{k} is the next concept.

concepts.recap: Each word asks (query), every word answers (key), softmax turns the matches into shares of one, and the word becomes a blend of the others' values in those shares.

concepts.title: Why divide by √d_k
concepts.idea: As word vectors get longer, raw match scores spread wider (their variance grows with the dimension d_k), which makes softmax put nearly all weight on one word and stalls learning, so dividing by √d_k keeps the weights sensible.

predict.question: Someone 'fixes' the problem a different way. With vectors of length 64 they divide every score by 64 instead of by √64 = 8. What happens to the weights?
options: They become nearly equal: every word gets about the same share
They come out the same as dividing by √64
One word still takes almost all the weight
They no longer add up to 100%
why: Right. The raw scores swing by about √64 = 8. Dividing by 64 squeezes that spread down to about 1/8. Softmax of near-identical scores gives near-identical weights, so the real match gets blurred away.
Tempting if any shrinking seems good enough. But 64 is eight times bigger than √64, so the scores end up eight times too squashed, not back at a spread of about 1.
That happens when scores are too spread out. Dividing by 64 makes them far less spread out, which pushes the weights the other way, toward equal.
Softmax always produces weights that sum to 100%, whatever scores you feed it. Scaling changes how the weight is shared out, never the total.

terms.means: The length of each query and key vector: how many numbers it holds. The paper uses 64.
A measure of how widely values swing: the typical spread, squared. Variance d_k means a typical spread of √d_k.
How much an output changes when an input is nudged. Training uses gradients to decide how to adjust the model, so tiny gradients mean almost no learning.
The paper's attention: dot-product scores divided by √d_k before softmax.

model.title: How the word 'sat' shares its attention in 'a cat sat on the mat'
model.note: Teaching model: one query word ('sat') and five other words with a fixed, invented pattern of match strengths. Raw scores are that pattern stretched by √length. This follows the paper's footnote: if query and key components are independent with mean 0 and variance 1, their dot product has variance d_k. Real scores are random and learned, not a fixed pattern. 'Learning signal' is 1 − Σw², the total sensitivity of the weights to small score changes; it stands in for gradient size. Numbers are illustrative, not the paper's data. The paper itself uses d_k = 64.

outputs.label: Biggest weight
outputs.expr: 1 / (1 + exp(-0.4 * spread) + exp(-0.9 * spread) + exp(-1.4 * spread) + exp(-2 * spread))

outputs.label: Learning signal
outputs.expr: 1 - top * top * (1 + exp(-0.8 * spread) + exp(-1.8 * spread) + exp(-2.8 * spread) + exp(-4 * spread))

steps.say: Each bar shows how much weight the word 'sat' gives to another word in 'a cat sat on the mat'. Together they always add up to 100%.
This slider sets how many numbers make up each query and key vector. Watch the bars as it moves.
This switch divides every match score by the square root of that length before softmax turns the scores into weights.
These readouts show how spread out the scores are, the biggest weight, and a learning signal: how much the weights can still shift when the scores are nudged.

explore.prompt: Now you drive. First push attention into collapse, then rescue it while keeping the vectors long.

goals.text: Make one word take more than 95% of the weight
hints: What turned the soft blend into winner-takes-all in the walkthrough?
Leave the dividing switch off and make the vectors longer, keeping an eye on the biggest weight.
It crosses 95% somewhere between the 16 and 256 the walkthrough visited.

goals.text: Use vectors longer than 100 numbers, yet keep the top word under half the weight
hints: On their own, long vectors make the scores spread wider. What can undo that?
The switch divides the scores by √length. Check the spread it leaves for softmax.
Slide the length past 100, then flip the switch.

feedback.correct: Yes. The goal is to bring the score spread back to about 1. Dividing by √d_k does exactly that. Dividing by d_k overshoots, squashing the scores so much that softmax spreads the weight almost evenly and the real match disappears.
feedback.incorrect: The scores swing by about √d_k, not d_k. Dividing by d_k = 64 shrinks the spread to about 1/8, far too small. Softmax of nearly equal scores gives nearly equal weights, so every word ends up with roughly the same share.

steps.say: Start with tiny vectors, one number each, and the switch off. 'cat' gets about 41% and 'mat' about 27%: a soft blend of several words.
Call the vector length d_k. A match score is a dot product: d_k products added together. Add 16 random-ish products and the total swings about 4 times wider.
The paper's footnote makes this exact. If each number has mean 0 and variance 1, the score's variance equals d_k. So its typical size grows like √d_k. At 64 that is 8 times wider.
Softmax turns score gaps into exponential ratios, so wider scores mean lopsided weights. 'cat' now takes about 96% and the other words almost vanish.
Look at the learning signal. When one weight is near 100%, nudging the scores barely moves the weights. The gradient is tiny, so training can hardly adjust anything. At 256 it is nearly zero.
Now flip the switch: divide every score by √d_k. The spread fed to softmax drops back to 1, however long the vectors are.
Even with 256 numbers per word, the weights are a soft blend again and the learning signal has recovered. This is scaled dot-product attention.

understand.explanation: A match score is a dot product: multiply a query and a key number by number, then add up all d_k products. Adding more of these products makes the total swing more widely. The paper's footnote shows that for components with mean 0 and variance 1, the score's variance is exactly d_k, so its typical size grows like √d_k. Softmax turns gaps between scores into exponential ratios, so wide scores hand almost all the weight to one word. Then small changes to the scores barely move the weights, and training gets tiny gradients. Dividing every score by √d_k brings the spread back to about 1 at any length. The authors present this as a suspected cause rather than a measured one: they cite earlier work showing that unscaled dot-product attention fell behind another kind of attention at large d_k, and they scale in their own model (d_k = 64) without reporting a test of the unscaled version.
understand.quote: While for small values of dk the two mechanisms perform similarly, additive attention outperforms dot product attention without scaling for larger values of dk [3]. We suspect that for large values of dk, the dot products grow large in magnitude, pushing the softmax function into regions where it has extremely small gradients

check.task: Put the model in the trouble state the paper warns about: the learning signal almost gone (below 0.05).
check.hint: Which switch setting lets the scores keep growing with length? Then ask how long the vectors must be before one word takes nearly everything.
check.misconception: That longer vectors only make matches sharper and more precise, at no cost. Without dividing, the extra spread makes softmax saturate and leaves almost nothing for training to work with.

connect.caption: This is Equation 1 of the paper. QK^{T} holds every query-key dot product, the raw scores whose spread grows like √d_k (blue, tied to the length slider and the raw spread readout). Dividing by √d_k (the switch) brings that spread back to about 1 before softmax makes the weights, which then blend the values V.

concepts.recap: Longer vectors make raw scores swing by about √d_k, so softmax crowns a single winner and learning stalls. Dividing by √d_k keeps the weights soft.

concepts.title: Many heads look for different things
concepts.idea: One attention head has to average everything it attends to into a single blend, while several smaller heads running side by side can each lock onto a different relationship.

predict.question: In the paper, the total size per word is fixed at 512 numbers and is split evenly among the heads. The base model uses 8 heads of 64 numbers each. Suppose you split it into 32 heads of only 16 numbers each. How did translation quality compare with the best setting?
options: Better: more heads can always pick out more relationships
A bit worse: each head becomes too small to judge matches well
Exactly as bad as a single head, since total computation is the same
No change at all from 8 heads
why: Tempting if more heads simply mean more relationships. But the heads share a fixed budget, so with 32 heads each one gets only 16 numbers. Table 3 shows quality fell to 25.4 BLEU, down from 25.8.

Right. Splitting helps up to a point. Past that, each head is too small to score matches well, and the paper also found that shrinking the key size d_k hurts quality. In Table 3, 32 heads scored 25.4 BLEU against 25.8 for 8 or 16 heads.
Equal computation does not mean equal quality. One head can only average, and it did worst of all (24.9 BLEU). 32 small heads still beat it (25.4).
Head count did matter in Table 3. The 32-head version came out 0.4 BLEU below the 8-head base model.

terms.means: One complete ask–match–blend unit: its own queries, keys and values, its own softmax weights, and one blended output
Several smaller attention heads running side by side, each free to look somewhere different, with their outputs joined together

model.title: Where each spotlight looks from the word 'its'
model.note: Teaching model: only four candidate words, a fixed match sharpness, and you set each spotlight's aim by hand. In the real Transformer, each head learns its own projections during training. Head size is ignored here: in the paper, splitting into more heads makes each one smaller. The sentence comes from the paper's Figure 4. The weights are illustrative, not the paper's data.

steps.say: Here is a sentence from the paper: 'The Law will never be perfect, but its application should be just.' To make sense of 'its', you need two other words: Law (whose?) and application (what?).
These first three bars show where spotlight 1 looks from 'its': at Law, at application, or at the other words. Together they always make 100%.
This slider swings spotlight 1 from Law toward application.
This switch adds a second spotlight. It has its own slider and its own three bars.
These two numbers show how clearly each word comes through: the biggest share any one spotlight gives it.

explore.prompt: First, see how far one spotlight can stretch to cover both words. Then use two and let each one specialise.

goals.text: With a single head, get both Law and application above 40% at the same time
hints: One head's weights must add up to 100%. How could two words both get a big share?
Look for the aim where the head favours neither word.
The two shares cross over between the Law-heavy aim and the application-heavy aim. Move in small steps and watch both numbers.

goals.text: Get both Law and application above 97% at once
hints: No single head can do this, because its weights add up to 100%.
Turn on the second head and give each head its own word.
A partial aim still leaks weight to the other words. Each head has to aim all the way at its word.

feedback.correct: Yes. More heads help only while each head stays big enough to judge matches. With the total size fixed, 32 heads of 16 numbers came out slightly worse than 8 or 16 heads, though still better than one head.
feedback.incorrect: You may have assumed more heads are always better, or that head count does not matter. In the paper, the heads split a fixed budget. One head can only average, but very many tiny heads each judge matches poorly, so quality peaked in the middle (Table 3, rows A).

steps.say: Start with one spotlight aimed at Law. The query from 'its' matches Law's key best, so softmax gives Law about 96%. Law comes through clearly, and application barely registers.
Swing it toward application. Now application is clear and Law nearly vanishes. The weights add up to one, so what one word gains, the other loses.

Aim in between. Both words get some weight, but the output is still one blend: mostly application with some Law stirred in. The two pieces of information are averaged into a single result and cannot be pulled apart.
This whole ask–match–blend unit is what the paper calls an attention head. One head gives one set of weights and one blend.
Now add a second head. If both heads aim at Law, the second just repeats the first, and application stays blurry. Extra heads only help if they look for different things.
Keep head 2 on Law and swing head 1 toward application. Law keeps its clear 96% through head 2, while application climbs in head 1. The two words no longer trade off against each other.
Running several heads side by side, each with its own queries, keys and values, is multi-head attention. Their outputs are joined rather than averaged, so each relationship keeps its own slot.

understand.explanation: A single attention head turns its match scores into weights that add up to one, and it outputs one weighted blend of values. If a word needs two different things (here 'its' needs its owner, Law, and the thing owned, application), one head must either pick one or average both into a single result where each is diluted. The Transformer instead runs several smaller heads in parallel, each with its own learned projections, and joins their outputs side by side, so each head can lock onto a different relationship. The base model uses 8 heads of 64 numbers each, which keeps total computation about the same as one full-size head. In English–German translation tests (Table 3), a single head scored 0.9 BLEU (a translation-quality score) worse than the best setting. The paper's attention pictures also show different heads apparently doing different jobs, though such pictures are suggestive rather than proof.
understand.quote: Multi-head attention allows the model to jointly attend to information from different representation subspaces at different positions. With a single attention head, averaging inhibits this.

connect.caption: This is the paper's equation. Each head_{i} is one full attention step with its own learned projections W_{i}^{Q}, W_{i}^{K}, W_{i}^{V}. Those projections decide where it looks, like the spotlight sliders (head 1 ↔ Spotlight 1, another head ↔ Spotlight 2). Concat places the heads' outputs side by side instead of averaging them, and W^{O} mixes them back to full size. The paper uses h = 8 heads; the model shows at most two.

concepts.recap: One head can only average what it attends to; several smaller heads side by side can each pick out a different relationship, though splitting too finely hurts too.

concepts.title: Giving word order back with waves
concepts.idea: Attention by itself cannot tell 'dog bites man' from 'man bites dog', so each word gets a position signal built from sine and cosine waves of different wavelengths, giving every position its own pattern.

predict.question: Imagine a version where every wave in the position signal was very slow, each taking tens of thousands of positions to rise and fall once. What would go wrong?
options: Neighbouring words would get almost the same pattern, so their order would be hard to read
Far-apart words would get the same pattern, because the waves repeat
Nothing: any wave still gives each position a slightly different pattern
Attention would stop working altogether
why: Right. A slow wave barely changes from one position to the next, just as the slow-wave difference was only about 0.10 for neighbours. With only slow waves, words 10 and 11 would look nearly identical. The fast waves are what separate neighbours.
This is the problem with fast waves, not slow ones. A very slow wave never comes back round within a sentence, so far-apart words are easy to separate. It is the close ones it blurs.

The patterns would differ, but only by tiny amounts between neighbours. A difference that small is hard for the network to pick up and use. The paper spreads wavelengths from 2π to 10000·2π so that both short and long distances show up clearly.
Attention would still match queries to keys and blend values as before. Only the clue about word order would get weak. The blending itself does not depend on the waves.

terms.means: A signal added to each word's vector that tells the model where in the sentence the word sits
How many positions a wave covers before it repeats its pattern

model.title: Waves that stamp each position with its own pattern
model.note: Teaching model: the base Transformer adds a 512-number position signal to every word. Here you see only 3 of those numbers: the sine waves for dimensions 0, 64 and 128 from the paper's formula with d_model = 512. Each sine has a cosine partner. The partners are hidden from the picture but included in the difference boxes. Positions are whole numbers from 0 (the first word) to 50. In the real model the signal is added to the word's own vector, not viewed alone. The differences are calculated from the formula and are not results reported in the paper.

steps.say: Left to right is a sentence: position 0 is the first word, then 1, 2, 3 and on. This wavy line rises and falls quickly as you move along it.
These two swing more slowly, and the green one slowest of all.
This slider places word A. Its line shows how high each wave is at that spot.
This one places word B.
The boxes show how differently each wave reads at A and at B. The switch turns the whole wave signal on or off.

explore.prompt: Move the two words around and find out which wave notices which kind of distance.

goals.text: Find two positions the fast wave can barely tell apart (difference under 0.2) while the slow wave tells them apart clearly (over 1).
hints: The fast wave keeps coming back to the same height. How far apart are its repeats?
Keep word A still and move word B away one step at a time. Watch the fast-wave difference dip and rise again.
The dips come roughly every six positions. You need one of the deeper dips a few repeats out, far enough that the slow wave has moved a long way.

goals.text: Find two different positions the slow wave can hardly tell apart (difference under 0.15), yet the whole pattern still separates clearly (over 0.9).
hints: Which wave barely changes over short distances?
Bring the two markers closer together and watch which difference boxes shrink and which stay large.
Get them as close as they can be without landing on the same spot.

feedback.correct: Yes. Slow waves change too little between next-door words to separate them. The fast waves are what tell neighbours apart, so a signal built only from slow waves would blur local order.
feedback.incorrect: You may have pictured slow waves repeating, but repeating is the fast waves' weakness. A slow wave hardly moves from one position to the next, so neighbours end up almost the same. That is why the paper mixes many wavelengths, from fast to very slow.

steps.say: Start with the signal off. Attention matches words by what they are, not where they are, so A and B carry no clue about place: difference 0. 'Dog bites man' and 'man bites dog' give each word the same blend.
Now switch it on. Every position gets a set of wave heights added to its word's vector. This added signal is called a positional encoding.
Put the words next door, at 10 and 11. The fast wave changes a lot in one step: its difference is about 0.96.
The slow wave hardly moves between neighbours: only about 0.10. For close words, the fast waves do the work.

Now move B out to 35, 25 places away. The fast wave repeats every 2π ≈ 6.3 positions. That distance is its wavelength. After about four repeats it is back near the same height, so its difference is only about 0.13.
The slow wave, with a wavelength near 63 positions, has not come back round. It now separates the words strongly, at about 1.90.
Read all the waves together, like the second, minute and hour hands of a clock. No two positions here share the same whole pattern, so every word carries a stamp of exactly where it sits.

understand.explanation: Attention compares words only by their content, so if you shuffle a sentence each word ends up with the same blend, and 'dog bites man' looks like 'man bites dog'. The Transformer fixes this by adding a position signal to every word's vector before attention starts. The signal is a stack of sine and cosine waves, with wavelengths growing step by step from about 6 positions to about 63,000 (2π to 10000·2π). Fast waves separate neighbours but repeat, so they confuse far-apart words. Slow waves do the reverse, and read together they give every position its own pattern. The authors also tried learned position vectors instead and got nearly identical translation scores (Table 3, row E: 25.7 vs 25.8 BLEU). They chose waves because they hoped, without testing it here, that waves would cope with sentences longer than any seen in training.
understand.quote: Since our model contains no recurrence and no convolution, in order for the model to make use of the order of the sequence, we must inject some information about the relative or absolute position of the tokens in the sequence.

check.task: Put the model in a state where words A and B sit at different positions, yet nothing the model sees tells their positions apart (whole-pattern difference below 0.01).
check.hint: Hunting for two positions with matching waves won't work in this range. Ask instead where the model's knowledge of position comes from in the first place.
check.misconception: Attention already knows word order because it compares every word with every other word, so positions would stay distinguishable even without the added wave signal.

connect.caption: This is the paper's formula from Section 3.5. 'pos' is a word's position, which you set with the sliders for words A and B. 'i' picks which pair of numbers in the signal you are looking at. With d_model = 512, dimension 0 is the fast wave (divide by 1), dimension 64 is the medium wave (divide by about 3.16), and dimension 128 is the slow wave (divide by 10). Each even dimension uses sine and the next odd one uses cosine. Together they make the full pattern behind the whole-pattern difference.

concepts.recap: Waves of many wavelengths, added to each word, give every position its own pattern: fast waves separate neighbours, slow waves separate distant words.

concepts.title: One step for any distance, and it wins
concepts.idea: Because self-attention links any two words in a constant number of steps and processes all words at once, the Transformer trained far faster than chain-based systems and still translated better.

predict.question: A self-attention layer reads a 2,000-word document in which the first and last words matter together. Compared with a 20-word sentence, what happens?
options: Linking them still takes one step, but the layer's total work grows a lot
Linking them takes about 100 times more steps, because the text is 100 times longer
Linking them takes one step, and the total work stays the same too
The layer cannot link words that far apart
why: Right. Every word looks at every other word directly, so the link stays one step. But the layer compares every pair of words, so its work grows with the square of the length (the paper's O(n²·d) per layer).
That is how the chain reader behaves: its steps grow with distance. The attention line stays flat because no word waits for a message passed along the chain.

The number of steps in a row stays flat, but the work does not. Comparing every pair of words means 10,000 times as many pairs here, which is why the paper suggests limiting attention to nearby words for very long inputs.
Distance does not block attention. Every position can attend to every other position in the same layer, however far apart they are.

terms.means: Attention in which the words of one sentence look at the other words of that same sentence
How many steps a signal must pass through to get from one word to another inside the network
A score of how closely a machine translation matches human reference translations; higher is better
Floating-point operations: a count of the total arithmetic a computer did, used here to measure training cost

model.title: Chain reader versus attention reader as a sentence grows
model.note: Teaching model: it counts only the steps that must happen one after another, and the hops needed to carry information between two words, for a single layer, as in the paper's Table 1 (O(n) for a recurrent layer, O(1) for self-attention). It ignores how long each step takes, constant factors, and the fact that a self-attention layer does more total work as sentences grow (O(n²·d) per layer). The flat attention line assumes hardware that can handle every word at once. The workers slider shows what a limited split looks like. Step counts are illustrative. The translation scores and training costs quoted in this concept are the paper's own (Table 2).

steps.say: This is the same picture as before. The solid line is the chain reader, taking one word after another. The dashed line is the same work with no chain, split among workers.
New: this flat line near the bottom is an attention reader. Every word looks straight at every other word at once, so it needs one step at any sentence length.
This box counts how many times longer the chain takes than attention to link your two words.

explore.prompt: Play with the two readers. Find where the chain hurts most, and work out what the no-chain split needs in order to keep up with attention.

goals.text: Find a sentence and a pair of words where the chain reader needs at least 20 times as many steps as attention to link them
hints: Which sliders decide how far the information has to travel along the chain?
Widening the distance alone may not work: two words can't be further apart than the sentence allows.
You need a sentence longer than 20 words, and two words at least 20 apart inside it.

goals.text: Make the no-chain split as fast as the attention reader, for a sentence the chain needs more than 5 steps to read
hints: Attention handles every word at the same moment. What would the split need for that?
The dashed line drops to a single step only when every word has its own worker.
Workers stop at a fixed maximum, so pick a sentence just over 5 words and at least as many workers as words.

feedback.correct: Yes. Distance never adds steps for attention, because every word looks at every other directly. The cost shows up elsewhere: one layer compares every pair of words, so its work grows with the square of the length.
feedback.incorrect: The chain's steps grow with distance, but attention's do not: any two words are one step apart. What does grow is the work inside the layer, because every pair of words gets compared. Long documents are expensive, not unreachable.

steps.say: Start small: a 10-word sentence, linking two words 3 apart. The chain passes the message along 3 times. Attention does it in 1.
Now link the first and last words. The chain needs 9 hand-offs. Attention still needs 1, because each word looks at the other directly.
The number of hops a signal must make between two words is called the path length. The paper argues that shorter paths make links between distant words easier to learn.
The flat line is self-attention: the words of one sentence attend to the other words of the same sentence, all in one layer, so the path length is 1 for any pair.
Reading the whole sentence works the same way. The chain must take 30 steps in a row. Attention computes all 30 words at once, as long as the hardware can handle them side by side.
Stretch to 60 words and link the two ends. The chain needs 59 hand-offs and 60 steps in a row. Attention: still 1. Fewer steps in a row means training can run in parallel on GPUs.
The paper measures training cost in FLOPs, the total arithmetic done. Its base Transformer trained in about 12 hours on 8 GPUs, using a fraction of the FLOPs of earlier systems.

Quality is scored in BLEU: the big Transformer hit 28.4 on English-to-German, over 2 points above the best before. Every word looking straight at every other word beat step-by-step reading, in a fraction of the training time.

understand.explanation: A recurrent network passes information along the chain, so linking two words far apart takes many hand-offs, and reading a sentence takes as many steps in a row as there are words. Self-attention lets every word look at every other word directly: any link is one step, and all words are processed at once (the paper's Table 1: O(1) versus O(n)). That gives short paths for long-range links and much more parallel work during training. The paper tested this on two translation benchmarks, where the Transformer matched or beat earlier systems at a much lower training cost. There is a price: each layer compares every pair of words, so its work grows with the square of the length. The authors note this is cheaper than a recurrent layer when sentences are shorter than the word-vector size, and suggest limiting attention to nearby words for very long inputs.
understand.quote: As noted in Table 1, a self-attention layer connects all positions with a constant number of sequentially executed operations, whereas a recurrent layer requires O(n) sequential operations.

equation.text: Steps in a row per layer: recurrent

connect.caption: This comes from the paper's Table 1 rather than a single equation, and n is the sentence length. The first O(n) is the solid chain line (steps in a row). The second O(n) is the chain's link line (hops between two words). Both O(1) terms are the flat attention line. Table 1 also lists the per-layer work: O(n²·d) for self-attention versus O(n·d²) for recurrent layers, the price attention pays for comparing every pair of words.

concepts.recap: Self-attention links any two words in one step and handles all words at once, so the Transformer trained faster and translated better, though per-layer work grows with length squared.

activities.prompt: Three rows from the paper's Table 2, all on the English-to-German test (newstest2014). Compare translation quality (BLEU) with training cost (FLOPs).

cases.label: GNMT + RL Ensemble (several recurrent models combined)
cases.text: BLEU 26.30. Training cost 1.8 × 10²⁰ FLOPs, about eight times more than the single model.

cases.label: Transformer (big)
cases.text: BLEU 28.4. Training cost 2.3 × 10¹⁹ FLOPs, the same budget as the single recurrent model. The smaller Transformer (base) scored 27.3 for 3.3 × 10¹⁸ FLOPs.

activities.takeaway: For the same training budget as one recurrent model, the big Transformer scored almost 4 BLEU higher. Even the cheap base model beat the expensive ensemble. The costs are the paper's estimates (training time × number of GPUs × each GPU's speed), not direct measurements.

activities.question: Which conclusion do the paper's results support?

options.text: Self-attention is cheaper than a recurrent layer for inputs of any length, even whole books.
options.feedback: Not supported. A self-attention layer compares every pair of words, so its work grows with the square of the length. The paper says it is faster when sentences are shorter than the word-vector size, and suggests restricting attention for very long inputs.

options.text: On these translation benchmarks, the Transformer scored better than the earlier systems in the table while using a fraction of their training cost.
options.feedback: Supported. Table 2 shows higher BLEU on English-to-German than every listed system, including ensembles, at much lower estimated FLOPs. The claim is limited to the tasks tested: two WMT 2014 translation tasks, plus a parsing test.

options.text: The one-step links alone explain the whole gain in quality.
options.feedback: Not shown. The Transformer differs from earlier systems in many ways (multiple heads, position signals, dropout, label smoothing, model size). Table 3 varies some of these parts, but no experiment isolates the one-step links as the single cause.

options.text: The Transformer understands sentences the way a person does.
options.feedback: Not supported. BLEU measures overlap with reference translations. Some attention patterns look related to sentence structure, but that is not evidence of human-like understanding.

hints: Separate what the tables measured from why the model works.
